danishChanges.before: Vi anser disse sandheder for selvindlysende: at alle mennesker er skabt lige; at de af deres Skaber er udstyret med visse umistelige rettigheder; at blandt disse er liv, frihed og stræben efter lykke. Klogskab tilsiger naturligvis, at længe etablerede regeringer ikke bør ændres af trivielle eller forbigående grunde. Al erfaring har vist, at menneskeheden hellere udholder lidelser, så længe ondet er til at bære, end retter op på forholdene ved at afskaffe de former, de er vant til. Men når et langvarigt mønster af overgreb og magtovertagelser, alle rettet mod samme mål, afslører en hensigt om at lægge folket under absolut despoti, da er det dets ret — og dets pligt — at afkaste en sådan regering og skabe nye værn for sin fremtidige sikkerhed. Den nuværende konge af Storbritanniens historie er en historie om gentagne overgreb og magtovertagelser, alle rettet mod at oprette absolut tyranni over disse stater. For at sikre disse rettigheder opretter mennesker regeringer, hvis retmæssige magt bygger på de regeredes samtykke. Når en styreform undergraver disse mål, har folket ret til at ændre eller afskaffe den og oprette en ny regering. Erfaringen viser da også, at mennesker hellere lider, så længe lidelserne er til at bære, end forbedrer deres vilkår ved at afskaffe de styreformer, de er vant til. Men når en lang række overgreb og uretmæssige magttiltag bestandigt sigter mod det samme og afslører en plan om at underkaste folket et uindskrænket despoti, er det folkets ret og pligt at styrte dette styre og skabe nye værn for sin fremtidige sikkerhed. englishChanges.before: Amendment XII. The electors will meet in their respective States and vote by ballot for President and Vice President — at least one of whom will not be an inhabitant of the same State as themselves. They will name in their ballots the person voted for as President, and in distinct ballots the person voted for as Vice President. They will make distinct lists of all persons voted for as President, and of all persons voted for as Vice President, and of the number of votes for each. The lists will be signed and certified and transmitted sealed to the seat of the government of the United States, directed to the President of the Senate. The President of the Senate will, in the presence of the Senate and House of Representatives, open all the certificates, and the votes will then be counted. The person having the greatest number of votes for President will be the President — if that number is a majority of the whole number of electors appointed. If no person has such a majority, then from the persons having the highest numbers (not exceeding three) on the list of those voted for as President, the House of Representatives will choose immediately, by ballot, the President. But in choosing the President, the votes will be taken by States — the representation from each State having one vote. A quorum for this purpose will consist of a member or members from two-thirds of the States, and a majority of all the States will be necessary to a choice. If the House of Representatives does not choose a President whenever the right of choice devolves upon them, before the fourth day of March next following, then the Vice President will act as President — as in the case of the death or other constitutional disability of the President. The person having the greatest number of votes as Vice President will be the Vice President — if that number is a majority of the whole number of electors appointed. If no person has a majority, then from the two highest numbers on the list, the Senate will choose the Vice President. A quorum for that purpose will consist of two-thirds of the whole number of Senators, and a majority of the whole number will be necessary to a choice. But no person constitutionally ineligible to the office of President will be eligible to that of Vice President of the United States.
englishChanges.after: Amendment XII. Electors meet in their own states and vote by ballot for President and Vice President. At least one candidate must live in a different state from the electors themselves. They name their presidential choice on one ballot and their vice-presidential choice on a separate ballot. They must draw up separate lists of everyone receiving presidential and vice-presidential votes, with each person's total. The lists must be signed, certified and sent sealed to the seat of the United States government, addressed to the President of the Senate. In the presence of the Senate and House of Representatives, the President of the Senate opens all the certificates and the votes are counted. The candidate with the most presidential votes becomes President if that total is a majority of all appointed electors. If no one has a majority, the House must immediately choose the President by ballot from no more than the three candidates with the most presidential votes. States vote separately, with each state's representatives collectively casting one vote. At least one member from each of two thirds of the states must be present, and election requires a majority of all states. If the House becomes responsible for the choice but has not chosen a President before the following 4 March, the Vice President acts as President, as on a President's death or other constitutional inability to serve. The candidate with the most vice-presidential votes becomes Vice President if that total is a majority of all appointed electors. If no one has a majority, the Senate chooses between the two candidates with the most votes. Two thirds of all Senators must be present, and election requires a majority of all Senators. Anyone constitutionally ineligible to be President is also ineligible to be Vice President.

Section 3. No person will be a Senator or Representative in Congress, or elector of President and Vice President, or hold any office (civil or military) under the United States, or under any State, who, having previously taken an oath as a member of Congress, or as an officer of the United States, or as a member of any State legislature, or as an executive or judicial officer of any State, to support the Constitution of the United States, has engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the same, or given aid or comfort to the enemies thereof. But neither the United States nor any State will assume or pay any debt or obligation incurred in aid of insurrection or rebellion against the United States, or any claim for the loss or emancipation of any slave; all such debts, obligations, and claims will be held illegal and void. englishChanges.after: Amendment XIV. Section 1. Everyone born or naturalised in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction is a citizen of the United States and of the state where they live. No one may serve as a Senator or Representative in Congress, a presidential or vice-presidential elector, or a civil or military officer of the United States or any state if, after previously swearing to support the United States Constitution, he has taken part in insurrection or rebellion against it or given aid or support to its enemies. Congress may remove this disqualification by a two-thirds vote in each House. Section 4. The validity of United States public debt authorised by law must not be questioned, including debts for pensions and bounties for service in suppressing insurrection or rebellion. But neither the United States nor any state may assume or pay debts or obligations incurred to support insurrection or rebellion against the United States, or claims for the loss or emancipation of slaves. All such debts, obligations and claims are illegal and void. Section 5. Congress may enforce this article's provisions through appropriate legislation.

englishChanges.before: Amendment XXV. Section 1. In case of the removal of the President from office, or of his death or resignation, the Vice President will become President. Section 2. Whenever there is a vacancy in the office of the Vice President, the President will nominate a Vice President — who will take office upon confirmation by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress. Whenever the President transmits to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives his written declaration that he is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office — and until he transmits to them a written declaration to the contrary — those powers and duties will be discharged by the Vice President as Acting President. Whenever the Vice President and a majority of either the principal officers of the executive departments, or of such other body as Congress may by law provide, transmit to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives their written declaration that the President is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office, the Vice President will immediately assume the powers and duties of the office as Acting President. Thereafter, when the President transmits to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives his written declaration that no inability exists, he will resume the powers and duties of his office — unless the Vice President and a majority of either the principal officers of the executive department, or of such other body as Congress may by law provide, transmit within four days to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives their written declaration that the President is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office. Thereupon Congress will decide the issue, assembling within forty-eight hours for that purpose if not in session. If the Congress, within twenty-one days after receipt of the latter written declaration — or, if Congress is not in session, within twenty-one days after Congress is required to assemble — determines by two-thirds vote of both Houses that the President is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office, the Vice President will continue to discharge the same as Acting President; otherwise, the President will resume the powers and duties of his office.
englishChanges.after: Amendment XXV. Section 1. If the President is removed, dies or resigns, the Vice President becomes President. Section 2. When the vice-presidency is vacant, the President nominates a Vice President, who takes office after confirmation by a majority in each House of Congress. Section 3. When the President sends the Senate's temporary presiding officer and the Speaker of the House his written declaration that he cannot carry out his office's powers and duties, the Vice President carries them out as Acting President. This continues until the President sends both officers a written declaration to the contrary. Section 4. If the Vice President, together with a majority of the executive department heads or of another body Congress establishes by law, sends both presiding officers a written declaration that the President cannot carry out his powers and duties, the Vice President immediately assumes them as Acting President. If the President then sends both officers a written declaration that he is able to serve, he resumes his powers and duties—unless, within four days, the Vice President and a majority of the department heads or the other body established by Congress send both officers a written declaration that he is still unable to serve. Congress must then decide the issue. If not in session, it must assemble within forty-eight hours for that purpose. If Congress determines by a two-thirds vote in each House that the President cannot carry out his powers and duties, the Vice President continues as Acting President. This decision must come within twenty-one days of receiving the second declaration or, if Congress was not in session, within twenty-one days of when it was required to assemble. Otherwise, the President resumes his powers and duties.
